spiritual_reading:
He teaches that there is an admission into living conjunction with the Divine and a containing form for tranquillity within the heavenly kingdom of wisdom. Yet the adversarial love of self, knowing that this admission is also the opening by which minds can be led out of infernal bondage, established within its ruling falsity a forbidding decree that none should turn to that Divine source, insinuating that whoever acknowledges it will lose life. It renamed the Divine shining as something destined to be extinguished, obstructed minds from directing their inner regard toward wisdom, and induced them to reject the very truth by which they are human.

He laments that people are in ignorance about spiritual realities. They have not recognized the magnitude of that Divine illuminating presence, have rejected its unmerited gift that is continually extended to them, and have not perceived its holiness. Nor have they understood the good it does for them even while they are still in the natural degree; for whenever spiritual wisdom flows down into their external life it is doing innumerable mercies for the human race, yet they deny benefits whose origin they do not acknowledge.

He says that whenever this Divine illuminating presence flows into the natural degree it brings a full course of complete operations in people, and they should be able to perceive them.

The first operation is enlightenment itself: it opens the understanding in all people so that they can discern in their conduct what lies before them and what they are doing. It removes the obscurity of falsity that had blinded them.

The second operation is tranquillity and peace: when wisdom is received into the life of the outer person it brings a calming order throughout, and it removes the anxieties and tremors that had filled the inner life during states of obscurity; for it dispels active falsity by truth, and by that quieting influx it extinguishes fear.

The third operation is awakening to spiritual vigilance: when illumination comes, those who were in spiritual sleep are roused into attention, and those who had been set to anxious guarding in ultimates cease from that strained watchfulness; for when truth is present, the outermost faculties that had been holding themselves on alert against unseen dangers relax into orderly use.

The fourth operation is fructification in the whole lower life: it gives nourishment and vigor, discernment and delight, to all perceptions and the works that proceed from them, and to all general and particular truths in the natural mind, and to all tender beginnings of good, throughout the whole extent of external life.

The fifth operation is the restraint of predatory evils: when enlightenment spreads through the outer person, malicious cravings and violent falsities that are full of harm withdraw into their hidden interiors.

The sixth operation is healing and the breaking of enchantment: when truth shines, the pain of spiritual injury is eased, and the deceptive practices by which the wicked act on others are dissolved.

The seventh operation is testimony and manifestation: it makes evident in the natural degree a sign that the heavenly kingdom of wisdom is real and present; for it is an outward witness of inward Divine splendour, and by it illumination is extended through the whole created mind.

He then grieves over how great the folly is that has seized those who are in falsified worship: they have not perceived the holy secret of this Divine illuminating presence, nor even the evident benefits it continually brings to them. They let these benefits pass without recognition.

He then teaches about the opposite state, the state of obscurity, because within it all evils find their opportunity. Whenever that obscurity descends upon the natural degree it brings a full course of complete infestations in people.

The first infestation is the spread of falsity: when illumination is withdrawn from the external mind and truth no longer acts there, obscurity immediately extends itself through the whole natural degree. People’s understanding is filled with denial and confusion; they neither discern nor rightly perceive, because falsity dominates the whole outer life.

The second infestation is fear: when obscurity strengthens, dread and trembling seize human minds, and the external life is filled with the oppressive presence of that state.

The third infestation is inward rebellion: when truth is absent, affections and thoughts rise up into disorder, and the heart turns toward doing evils and rushing into spiritual ruin.

The fourth infestation is spiritual stupor: a heavy torpor settles on people; they fall into negligence, listlessness, and a deathlike insensibility in respect to what is living.

The fifth infestation is the concealment and distortion of what is human: when falsity covers the outer life, the distinct form of each person’s quality is hidden; mutual recognition of what is good and true between people is obscured, and what should appear as spiritual beauty is not manifested.

The sixth infestation is the empowerment of evildoing: as soon as obscurity is allowed to rule, those who love evil come forth into action—those who profane good, those who steal truth for self, those who secretly poison the understanding. Then bestial affections and crawling falsities rise from hidden loves and begin to prowl in the external life. Infernal influences also find greater power for operation. Then conflicts, assaults, injuries, and outpourings of harm torment people, because in that state every evil is strengthened.

The seventh infestation is the manifestation of infernal origin: the state of obscurity displays in the natural degree a sign of the active falsity from which it proceeds, because this obscurity is an effect of primal denial made present in external life. This effect is intertwined with and binds together disordered things in both higher and lower regions of the mind.

He says he has taught these complete infestations of obscurity that occur repeatedly in the natural degree. Those who are in falsified worship have not understood what this state is, nor the source from which it draws its power—that all these evils are strengthened within it.

He then says there are sufficient universal qualities present in enlightenment as it acts in the external life.

The first is illumination: by it the natural mind and all affections and thoughts within it are made able to see.

The second is spiritual beauty: when illumination is present it pours a kind of loveliness and attractiveness into affections and thoughts, ordering them into a pleasing form.

The third is peace: when truth from wisdom is received, people take on gentler affection through it and come into mutual concord.

The fourth is liberation of the living mind: it releases the inner life from the constraints imposed by both higher and lower bondage—that is, from compulsions in the spiritual degree and from entanglements in the natural degree—so that it can act from freedom according to order.

The fifth is strengthening in ultimates and delight in the whole complex of doctrine: it gives power to the fundamental receptacles of life, and it gives perception and pleasantness to the entire structure of saving truth that bears witness to Divine love and wisdom.

He insists that these qualities are pre-eminent: the illumination is greater than any lesser understanding that appears in the natural degree; the beauty it imparts surpasses merely natural attractiveness; its peace excels all merely external securities that people set up. The liberation it brings to the living mind is beyond all other modes of release. The strength it supplies to the operative powers in ultimates surpasses every natural power.

He then says that, in addition, there are further universal marks made evident by enlightenment that disclose something of the mystery of the First Divine.

The first is unceasing plenitude: the receptive form through which this illumination acts is continually filled and does not diminish by alternations the way lower, derivative illumination does. This constant fullness manifests that the Divine Source is inexhaustible, from whom all capacities and all objects of worship in the mind proceed. In the Divine there is no waning and no lack.

The second is incomparable supremacy of wisdom: the illumination that descends from this source exceeds all lesser truths and all derivative lights in the whole mental universe, because it bears witness that the Divine Light surpasses the light of even the heavenly degrees.

The third is transcendence of state: this illumination stands in a higher degree than all elevated natural states, and surpasses every exalted condition that can be attained in the external life. This manifests that the Divine is above the whole ordered heaven of wisdom, above all heights of spiritual life, and is perpetually in the fullness of His own likeness from eternity to eternity.

He declares that he has taught two mysteries that appear repeatedly in the created mind: the mystery of enlightenment and the mystery of obscurity. These are made visible in order each day, yet those who are in error have not recognized them.

He says that the primary mystery of Divine illumination is made present in the natural degree as a secondary source of enlightenment that comes continually into the outer life. It shows in all its operations that it is good, proceeding from good itself. It comes from the good Divine Source and becomes apparent in external existence.

In contrast, the state of obscurity, which is full of fear, exists from the mystery of active falsity. It too displays its origin in external life by all these evils. It manifests this mystery continually, yet those who are in error do not know it; they do not distinguish the mystery of enlightenment from the mystery of obscurity.

He teaches that those who receive and live from illumination are born from it and belong to it; but those who take on the quality of obscurity are born from that state and belong to it.

He pronounces blessed those who have learned to recognize these states within themselves: that enlightenment comes from the Divine Light, and obscurity from active falsity; and that they do not arise from one another. Blessed is the person who can know this distinction and discern these two origins—good with its truth, and evil with its falsity—as not derived one from the other; for by this discernment the mind can be led into eternal life.

fills.fill: which comes daily to the world
fills.notes: The passage identifies the great light-giver (the sun) as a cosmic ‘gate’ and ‘vessel’ for the aeon of Light, and immediately turns to Satan’s prohibition of worshipping it. The oldest-layer logic regularly defines the sun here as the daily appearing emissary of the Light-realm, so the missing clause should specify its recurrent descent into the world, not a devotional epithet.

The sentence is a heading-like transition: it first announces ‘There are five archetypes occur in the sun’, then must restate that the sun ‘makes them apparent’ or ‘manifests them’ in the world. Since the object is already ‘five archetypes’, the lacuna supplies that direct object again in idiomatic Coptic-English: ‘it making them five archetypes as it finds the world’ = ‘manifesting these five archetypes upon the world as it is’.

The intended sense is continuous plenitude: ‘filled up in his image every time and every hour’. ‘All the time’ is an editor’s smoothing; the substrate idiom is ‘every time and every hour’, stressing unceasing renewal in discrete moments.

The contrast requires a conditional uptake of quality: those who are ‘children of day and light’ versus those who assume the opposite quality and so belong to night and darkness. The oldest register speaks impersonally of ‘taking up’ or ‘putting on’ a nature, aligning with the correspondential point that one becomes of that state by reception, not by lineage or exhortation.

assessment: Most gaps are short and structurally constrained by the chapter’s parallelism (day seven goods, night seven evils; then five and three ‘archetypes’). ¶32 and ¶33 are tightly determined. ¶2 and ¶22 require brief formulaic clauses typical of this cosmological instruction and are recoverable with moderate confidence. ¶37 is least constrained because the surviving English already contains an interpolated gloss; the restoration supplies the minimal substrate-style conditional needed to complete the antithesis.
